title: Hazy Lager Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What a hazy lager is, why brewers dry hop lager and leave it cloudy and how it differs from a hazy IPA or a classic pilsner.
teaser: Lager yeast, IPA hops and no filter. Hazy lager is one of craft beer's newer hybrids.
standfirst: Hazy lager takes the soft, juicy hop character of a hazy IPA and puts it on a clean lager base. It is cloudy, aromatic and usually around 5 to 6% ABV. Here is how brewers make it and what to look for when you taste one.
sections:
For most of brewing history, lager meant clear beer. Brewers filtered it, lagered it cold for weeks and aimed for brilliant clarity. Hazy lager throws that out. It uses lager yeast and cool fermentation, then adds the hop treatment of a New England IPA: heavy late hopping, dry hopping and no filtration.

There is no official guideline yet. Brewers use the name for a range of beers, usually 5 to 6% ABV, with low to moderate bitterness and strong hop aroma. It sits alongside other hybrids such as the cold IPA and the India pale lager.

The cloudiness has several sources. Grains such as oats and wheat add proteins and other compounds that stay in suspension. Heavy dry hopping adds polyphenols, which bind with proteins to form a stable haze. Skipping filtration leaves fine particles in the beer. Our guide to hazy versus clear beer explains the chemistry.

Haze is meant to be stable in this style. A hazy lager should look evenly cloudy, not like a glass of muddy water with chunks floating in it. Visible particles or yeast clumps suggest a production problem rather than style.

Lager yeast ferments cool, typically around 8 to 13 °C. It produces few fruity esters. That gives hazy lager a cleaner base than a hazy IPA, where ale yeasts often add their own peach or stone fruit notes. The hops do all the talking.

Cool fermentation brings its own challenges. Lager yeast can leave sulphur or diacetyl if not given time and the right temperature to clean up. Many brewers raise the temperature near the end of fermentation for a few days, a diacetyl rest, before cooling. Rushing a hazy lager to market risks buttery or eggy notes under the hops.

That time costs money. A hazy IPA might be ready in two to three weeks, while a hazy lager often needs four to six once fermentation, rest and a short cold conditioning are added up. For a small brewpub with only a few fermenters, that is a real trade-off. Some brewers choose to sell a hazy lager only in cooler months, when tank pressure is lower.

Dry hopping a lager is trickier than dry hopping an ale. At lower temperatures, hop oils dissolve more slowly, so brewers may need longer contact or more hops. Dry hopping rates can reach several grams per litre.

Dry hops also bring enzymes that can break down some of the sugars yeast could not ferment. That restarts fermentation in the tank, a process known as hop creep. It can raise alcohol slightly, dry the beer out and produce diacetyl late in the process. Lager brewers watch for this closely, because lager yeast at cold temperatures is slow to clean it up.

A good hazy lager is soft, juicy and crisp at the same time. Aroma shows tropical fruit, citrus or stone fruit from modern hops. The body is smooth, helped by oats or wheat. Bitterness is gentle, usually low to moderate. The finish should be clean and fairly dry, with none of the sweet ester heaviness of some hazy IPAs.

Watch for faults. Butter or butterscotch points to diacetyl. Rotten egg or struck match points to excess sulphur. Harsh, grassy or vegetal bitterness suggests too many hops left too long. A thick, chewy body is more hazy IPA than hazy lager.

Hazy beers are fragile. The hop aromas that define them fade quickly with heat and oxygen. In Indian conditions, where cans can sit warm in trucks and shops, a hazy lager can lose its brightness within weeks. Oxidised hazy beer can also darken and taste muddy or cardboard-like.

Buy from places that keep beer cold, check the packaging date and drink it soon. Serve around 5 to 7 °C in a straight glass. For brewers, it is a strong case for a short supply chain: hazy lager suits taproom pours far better than long-distance distribution.

Hazy lager tests a taster's ability to look under the hops. Strong aroma can hide faults such as diacetyl or sulphur. Spotting them and telling hop fruit from yeast fruit are skills that come with guided tasting against reference samples.

For a first step, pour a hazy lager next to a clear pilsner and a hazy IPA. Taste the pilsner first, then the hazy lager, then the IPA. Note where the hazy lager sits in body, bitterness and fruit. You will learn what the lager yeast is contributing.
faqs: A hazy lager is an unfiltered lager made with lager yeast and heavy late and dry hopping, giving a cloudy, juicy beer around 5 to 6% ABV.
Is hazy lager the same as a hazy IPA?
No. It uses lager yeast and cool fermentation, which gives a cleaner base with fewer fruity esters than a hazy IPA.
Proteins from oats and wheat bind with polyphenols from heavy dry hopping. The beer is also left unfiltered.
Does hazy lager go stale quickly?
Yes. Its hop aromas fade fast with heat and oxygen, so drink it fresh and keep it cold.
